deck: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods

cards.front: In which package does String live, and why does it need no import?
cards.back: java.lang — every compilation unit imports that package implicitly
cards.extra: The JLS states that every compilation unit implicitly imports every public class of the predefined package java.lang, as if import java.lang.*; appeared right after the package declaration. That is why String, System and Math resolve with no import while ArrayList does not.
cards.example:
// ArrayList needs an import, String does not
import java.util.ArrayList;

String s = new String();   // java.lang, already visible

cards.front: How do you get the length of a String, and how does it differ from an array?
cards.back: s.length() is a method; an array's a.length is a field
cards.extra: The length of an array is a public final field (§10.7), so a.length compiles and a.length() does not. String exposes length as a method instead, so the parentheses are mandatory there and s.length alone is a compile error.
cards.example:
String s = "hello";
s.length();   // 5 - method call

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
a.length;     // 3 - field, no parentheses

cards.front: Do two identical string literals refer to the same object?
cards.back: Yes — literals are interned and share one instance
cards.extra: JLS §3.10.5 says a string literal always refers to the same instance of class String, because literal and constant-expression strings are interned as if by String.intern(). So "a" == "a" is true, but new String("a") == "a" is false — the constructor builds a second object.
cards.example:
String a = "hi";
String b = "hi";
System.out.println(a == b);              // true
System.out.println(a == new String("hi")); // false
